title: Codeword-to-layer mapping for the NR downlink with a hand-grip model
subtitle: System-level results: FTP model 1, Dense Urban-eMBB, 20 MHz, MMSE-IRC receiver

blocks.p: With the users' hand grip modelled and a fair NR baseline, both multi-codeword mappings give a small but consistent gain in mean user-perceived throughput (UPT) over NR's single codeword with an MMSE-IRC receiver: **about 2 % at every load with sub-band SVD precoding**, and 1.5–2 % at 20 and 50 % load but under 1 % at 70 % load with wideband SVD.

blocks.cap: Table 1. Mean UPT gain over NR's single codeword with the hand grip modelled. Mean over the files of 10 drops; ± is the standard error of the 10 single-drop gains (every scheme sees the same users, channels and files in a drop).

b: **Consistency.** 109 of the 120 single-drop gains are positive; with sub-band SVD, 57 of 60. The worst single drop is −1.9 %.
**LTE style against one codeword per layer.** They are equal within the noise: they differ by at most half a point of mean UPT. LTE style gets there with two codewords instead of four.
**Cell edge.** The 5th-percentile UPT gains +0.5 to +3.7 % with sub-band SVD. With wideband SVD it gains at 20 and 50 % load and is flat to −1.3 % at 70 %.

**The hand grip itself changes little.** It raises the multi-codeword gain by about a third of a point on average, most clearly with sub-band SVD at 50 and 70 % load (+1.1 → +1.9 % and +1.3 → +2.3 % for LTE style).
**Against the 2–5 % target.** Sub-band SVD reaches the lower end of it at all three loads. More than that is not available with MMSE-IRC; it needs a receiver that cancels codewords (section 6).
**Placeholder values.** The 6 dB hand loss on one or two covered antennas is an assumption of this study, not a specified or measured value (section 3).

blocks.p: Three ways of mapping codewords to up to four MIMO layers are compared in the same system simulation. Each codeword has its own MCS, CQI, HARQ process and ACK/NACK.

The assumptions are those of the earlier FTP model 1 evaluation at 20 MHz, with three changes: the hand grip of section 3, the fair baseline (below), and arrival rates calibrated for exactly this configuration.

blocks.p: **Fair baseline.** In the earlier runs NR had one OLLA loop per user for all ranks, while the multi-codeword schemes had one per codeword. A loop per rank is something NR can do just as well, and it makes NR itself 3–4 % faster; without it, part of the multi-codeword gain is only better link adaptation. The 4-slot HARQ round trip is the shorter of the two values studied; with several codewords a file more often ends on a retransmission of a single codeword, so a long round trip costs the multi-codeword schemes more.

blocks.p: The grip has two parts. The first is from TR 38.901; the second is an addition of this study, because the first cannot make one UT antenna weaker than another.

blocks.p: **The 6 dB and the number of covered antennas are placeholders.** They are not from a specification or a measurement and should be replaced by agreed values. The 30 dB of the self-blocking is the fixed value of TR 38.901.
What the grip does to the channel, measured on the singular values of each user's serving channel (4 × 32, two drops, 2,280 users):

blocks.cap: Table 6. Median gap of each layer's singular value to the strongest layer.

b: **Self-blocking.** It costs a user 2.4 dB of received power on average and 1.1 dB at the median, after the user has picked its best cell; a quarter of the serving-cell clusters are blocked. It widens the gap of layers 3 and 4 by about 1 dB.
**Hand loss.** 6 dB on one or two antennas falls mostly on the weakest layer: the gap of layer 4 widens by another 2.3 dB, that of layer 2 by 0.5 dB.

blocks.cap: Figure 1. Mean UPT gain over NR with the hand grip. Large dot: all files of the 10 drops; bar: 95 % confidence interval from the 10 single-drop gains; small dots: the single drops.

blocks.p: With sub-band SVD the gain is about 2 % at all three loads and four to eight standard errors above zero. With wideband SVD it is 1.5–2 % at 20 and 50 % load and drops to 0.8 % at 70 %, where it is still about two standard errors above zero. The two mappings never differ by more than half a point, which is about one standard error.

blocks.cap: Table 7. UPT gain over NR at the mean, 5th and 95th percentile of the files, and the range of the single drops' mean gains.

blocks.p: The percentiles are noisier than the mean, because they rest on fewer files. With sub-band SVD neither end of the distribution loses: the 5th percentile gains at every load, and the 95th percentile is flat at 20 % load and gains 2–4 % at 50 and 70 %. With wideband SVD at 70 % load the cell-edge users are flat with LTE style and 1.3 % slower with one codeword per layer.

blocks.cap: Table 8. Absolute numbers of the three schemes. BLER is that of first transmissions, per codeword in the order of the layers; the retransmission share is the share of scheduled RBGs that carried retransmissions.

blocks.p: Three things stand out. **Rank.** The multi-codeword schemes use rank 4 more often than NR (43 and 37 % against 29 % of the transmissions with sub-band SVD at 20 % load), because a weak fourth layer only lowers the MCS of its own codeword. **BLER.** Every codeword sits near the 10 % target; the third and fourth codewords of one codeword per layer, which carry the weakest layers, are 1–3 points higher. **Retransmissions.** They take a larger share of the resources with more codewords, 12 and 14 % against 7 % of the RBGs at 70 % load, which offsets part of the gain.

blocks.cap: Table 9. Without the grip → with the grip, fair baseline in both. The runs without the grip used arrival rates calibrated for the earlier baseline, so their load is a little lower. The two sides are different users and files and are compared as averages only.

blocks.p: At 20 % load NR is 3–4 % slower with the grip than without, and at 50 and 70 % load 0–2 % slower; part of this is the 3–5 % higher arrival rate of the runs with the grip. NR's rank-4 share falls by 4 points at 20 % load. The multi-codeword gain rises in 8 of the 12 cells and falls in 4, by +0.35 points on average; a single cell's change (−0.7 to +1.2 points) is within two standard errors of such a difference, about 0.6 points each. So the grip, with a 6 dB hand loss, does not change the picture: it makes the fourth layer 3.6 dB weaker (Table 6), but most transmissions do not use the fourth layer.

b: **MMSE-IRC, sub-band (reciprocity-based) precoding.** LTE style and one codeword per layer gain 2.0–2.4 % mean UPT over NR at 20, 50 and 70 % load with the hand grip, in 57 of 60 single drops, without a loss at the cell edge.
**MMSE-IRC, wideband precoding.** 1.5–2.0 % at 20 and 50 % load, 0.8 % at 70 %.
**Number of codewords.** Two codewords (LTE style) give the gain of four within half a point. Nothing here argues for more than two.
**Hand grip.** With TR 38.901 self-blocking and a 6 dB hand loss, the gain is about a third of a point higher than without the grip. The conclusion does not depend on the grip.
**Size of the gain.** About 2 % is what MMSE-IRC supports when NR's link adaptation is given the same per-rank outer loop. A larger gain needs codeword-level interference cancellation.
**Hand-loss values.** 6 dB on 1 or 2 antennas is a placeholder (section 3). The gain of the multi-codeword schemes is expected to grow with the loss; this has not been swept at system level.

**Hand-loss model.** One loss for every covered antenna, the same at all frequencies, no change of the antenna pattern, and no link between which antennas are covered and which directions are blocked.

**Receiver.** MMSE-IRC only. A codeword-level SIC receiver is where multiple codewords gain most (+5 to +12 % mean UPT in the earlier FTP model 3 runs with ideal cancellation); it has not been rerun with the fair baseline and the grip.

**Baseline.** NR here has per-rank OLLA and a 2 ms HARQ round trip. With one loop for all ranks or an 8-slot round trip the comparison shifts: see the earlier results in results/cw2lm_ftp1_fair_20mhz.md.
**Load.** The evaluation runs land at 19, 44–45 and 67 % RU, not 20, 50 and 70 %: they are shorter than the calibration runs and start from an empty system.
**Statistics.** 10 drops, 1,400 to 5,400 files per cell of Table 1. The standard error of a mean gain is 0.3–0.6 points; differences between the two multi-codeword schemes are within the noise.

**Reference without the grip.** It ran at a slightly lower load (17–18, 44 and 65 % RU) and with a scheduler buffer-estimate cap of 7.406 instead of 7.4 bit per RE and layer, which moves a run's mean UPT by at most 0.5 %.
